Swag Std.Core

Core is the foundation library shared by Swag applications and standard modules. It provides owned collections and strings, text and Unicode processing, files and paths, serialization, mathematics, hashing, cryptography, time, concurrency, reflection, diagnostics, input, and access to the host environment.

The APIs are grouped into focused namespaces such as Core.Math, Core.File, Core.Path, Core.Time, Core.Threading, Core.Sync, Core.Serialization, Core.Globalization, Core.Scc, Core.Crypto, and Core.Reflection. Frequently used value types, including Core.Array, Core.HashTable, Core.OrderedMap, Core.OrderedSet, Core.Deque, Core.PriorityQueue, and Core.String, live directly in Core.

Read and process a file

using Core let text = try File.readAllText("settings.txt") var lines: Array'String for line in text.splitLines() do lines.add(line)

Owned containers release their storage automatically. Slices and string views borrow storage instead; keep their source alive and do not retain them across an operation that can reallocate that source.

Derive short-lived key material

using Core let password = cast(const [..] u8) "password" let salt = cast(const [..] u8) "application salt" var key: [32] u8 defer Crypto.secureClear(key) try Crypto.pbkdf2HmacSha256(password, salt, 200_000, key)

Cryptographic randomness and guaranteed clearing use the target operating system behind the portable Core.Crypto API.

Store independently readable payloads

Core.Scc writes a versioned Swag Chunk Container whose manifest remains cheap to read. Each payload has a stable type, role, codec, checksum, and file range, so an application can load a thumbnail or metadata chunk without reading the main document.

using Core let profile = try Guid128.parse("fc9456cf-5ec9-4710-bd12-b6bdd64a77a5") let role = try Guid128.parse("582e4036-ee6f-45b5-86d9-7972bb7e0a19") var writer: Scc.Writer writer.initialize(profile) let previewId = try writer.addChunk("preview bytes", {roleId: role}) try writer.saveAtomic("capture.scc") var reader: Scc.Reader try reader.initialize("capture.scc") let preview = try reader.readChunk(previewId)

Core at a glance

Core supplies the building blocks used throughout the standard workspace. Pick an area by the problem you need to solve:

GoalStart with
Store an ordered sequenceCore.Array or Core.StaticArray
Associate keys with valuesCore.HashTable, Core.HashSet, Core.OrderedMap, or Core.OrderedSet
Work at both sequence endsCore.Deque
Consume work by priorityCore.PriorityQueue
Own and edit UTF-8 textCore.String
Inspect borrowed UTF-8 dataCore.Utf8 and slices
Work with files and pathsCore.File, Core.Directory, and Core.Path
Encode structured dataCore.Serialization
Measure time or datesCore.Time
Run concurrent workSwag.Task, Core.Threading, and Core.Sync
Inspect types at runtimeCore.Reflection
Hash or checksum bytesCore.Hash

Most Core types are ordinary values with deterministic cleanup. Collections and strings own their buffers; copying them copies their content. Pointer and slice fields are commonly borrowed views, so their declaring type documents the corresponding lifetime.

Operations that can fail use Swag's fail mechanism. Propagate a failure with try, or catch it at the boundary where the program can add useful context.

Collections and borrowing

Core.Array is the default growable sequence. Core.HashTable provides key-value lookup, Core.HashSet stores unique keys, and Core.StaticArray keeps a sequence inline with a fixed maximum capacity. Core.OrderedMap and Core.OrderedSet trade insertion cost for sorted traversal and range queries. Core.Deque serves both ends of a sequence, while Core.PriorityQueue exposes the next element selected by a comparator.

using Core var names: Array'String names.add("Ada") names.add("Grace") var scores: HashTable'(String, u32) scores.add("Ada", 10) scores.add("Grace", 12) if let entry = scores.tryFind("Ada") do Console.printLn(entry.value)

Ordering and ranges

Ordered collections and priority queues take an explicit comparator. Its arguments are borrowed. Return a negative value when the left argument belongs before the right argument, zero when their ordering keys are equal, and a positive value otherwise.

var ranking: OrderedMap'(u32, String) ranking.initialize(func(left, right: const *u32)->s32 => left[] <=> right[]) ranking.add(20, "silver") ranking.add(10, "gold") for entry in ranking.range(10, 30) do Console.printLn(entry.key, ": ", entry.value) var work: PriorityQueue'u32 work.initialize(func(left, right: const *u32)->s32 => left[] <=> right[]) work.push(30) work.push(10) let first = work.pop()

Ranges are half-open: range(lower, upper) contains keys greater than or equal to lower and less than upper. A range is a borrowed slice and is invalidated by insertion or removal.

Ownership rule

An owning collection controls its elements and buffer. A slice returned by toSlice, range, a pointer returned by lookup, or an iterator variable borrows that storage. Adding, removing, resizing, clearing, or freeing the collection can invalidate those borrowed values.

Prefer a slice when a function only needs temporary sequential access. Prefer an owned collection when the callee must retain or modify the data independently.

Use Core.Deque.frontPtr, Core.Deque.backPtr, or Core.PriorityQueue.peekPtr to inspect an element without copying it. Their read-only overloads also work when the element owns a resource and cannot be copied. Borrowing either end of a deque does not allocate or move its elements.

Capacity and reuse

Repeated insertion can grow a collection. Reserve capacity before a known batch when pointer stability or allocation cost matters, and use clear when the allocation should be retained for reuse. Use free when the capacity itself should be returned immediately.

For Core.Deque, Core.PriorityQueue, Core.OrderedMap, and Core.OrderedSet, reserving zero or an already available capacity leaves elements and storage intact. Core.Array.reserve has a different, explicit zero-capacity contract: reserve(0) releases its storage and removes all elements, just like Core.Array.free.

Building byte buffers

Core.ConcatBuffer owns a chain of byte buckets and supports a write cursor. Writes overwrite existing bytes at that cursor and extend the buffer when needed. Core.ConcatBuffer.reserveInPlace returns contiguous storage to fill directly; crossing an existing bucket boundary merges the content and invalidates borrowed positions and pointers. Save a Core.ConcatBufferPosition only while its bucket storage remains valid.

clear retains the buckets for reuse; release frees them and leaves the buffer reusable with the same allocator and bucket size. The buffer can be moved with #move, but implicit copies are rejected. Moving an embedded first bucket also invalidates positions borrowed from that header.

Core.ConcatBuffer.toArray copies all bytes into an independently owned array without merging buckets or moving the cursor. Use it when an API needs one contiguous owned block, such as an encoded image or video payload.

Core.ConcatBuffer.toString copies the content. Core.ConcatBuffer.moveToString consumes a single heap bucket and returns an owned, null-terminated string; it copies multiple active buckets or an embedded first bucket, leaving the buffer intact. Use Core.ConcatBuffer.toSlice for a temporary borrow when one active bucket holds the content. Its const overload exposes read-only bytes.

Text and Unicode

Core.String owns mutable UTF-8 bytes. A Swag string or byte slice can refer to existing storage without owning it. Use the owning type when text must survive changes to its source.

The text namespaces separate operations by encoding:

Encoding or taskAPI
UTF-8 traversal and validationCore.Utf8
UTF-16 conversionCore.Utf16
Unicode categories and case mappingCore.Unicode
Latin-1 classificationCore.Latin1
Numeric and value conversionCore.StrConv
Placeholder-based formattingCore.Format
TokenizationCore.Tokenize
Regular expressionsCore.Parser.RegExp

Indexing UTF-8 by byte is appropriate for ASCII delimiters and encoded storage, but not for counting displayed characters. Decode runes when character boundaries matter, and keep byte offsets when slicing the original UTF-8 value.

Formatting creates text for display; parsing converts text back to typed values. Keep machine-readable formats independent of locale unless a declaration explicitly accepts globalization settings.

Files, paths, and serialization

Core.Path manipulates path text without accessing the filesystem. Core.File and Core.Directory perform filesystem operations. Core.File.FileStream, Core.ByteStream, Core.ByteSource, Core.ByteSink, and Core.File.TextReader support incremental I/O.

using Core let configPath = Path.combine("config", "application.json") if File.exists(configPath) { let source = try File.readAllText(configPath) // Decode the source at the application boundary. }

Use whole-file helpers for small resources and configuration. Prefer streams for large files, bounded memory use, or processing that can start before the complete file is available.

Decoding a file of any size

Core.ByteSource and Core.ByteSink are what a codec reads and writes through. Each has a file backing and a memory backing behind the same operations, so a decoder written once reads a ten-hour recording and a byte slice alike, and a file source holds one read window whatever the length of the file. A read larger than the window goes straight to its destination; Core.ByteSource.peek lends the bytes ahead of the read position without copying them, which is how a walker over frame headers scans a file at the cost of its index.

using Core var source = try ByteSource.openFile("recording.mp3") while not source.isAtEnd() { let header = try source.peek(4) let length = frameLength(header) try source.skip(length) }

A container writer reserves the totals of its header and fills them in once the last frame has landed: Core.ByteSink.patch rewrites bytes the sink already accepted, so writing a long stream costs the memory of one frame rather than the memory of the result.

using Core var sink = try ByteSink.createFile("clip.avi") let sizeField = sink.position() try sink.writeLittleEndian(0'u32) // ... frames ... try sink.patch(sizeField, sizeBytes) try sink.close()

Memory-mapped files

Core.File.MappedFile creates independently owned Core.File.MappedRegion views for random access to large files. A region may start at any byte offset; the platform alignment is handled internally.

using Core var file = try File.MappedFile.open("archive.bin", .ReadWrite) var header = try file.map(0, 4096) header.writableBytes()[0] = 1 try header.flush()

Close all regions before resizing. A region remains usable if its source Core.File.MappedFile is closed, but its byte slices become invalid as soon as the region itself closes. CopyOnWrite regions are writable private copies; their changes are intentionally never persisted.

Watching a directory

Core.Directory.Watcher provides a cancellable stream for tools that react to file edits. Each read has an explicit Core.Directory.WatchStatus: changes, timeout, overflow, or cancellation.

using Core var options: Directory.WatchOptions options.recurse = true var watcher = try Directory.watch("sources", options) for { let batch = try watcher.next(1000) if batch.status == .Overflow { // Rescan the complete tree because native records were lost. continue } if batch.status == .Cancelled do break for change in batch.changes do Log.write(change.path) }

Rename records are paired even when a host buffer boundary splits them. A timeout leaves the native request pending, so repeated timed reads do not create a notification gap. Call cancel from another thread to wake an unbounded next; call close only after the reading thread has returned.

Structured data

Core.Serialization provides a shared traversal model with JSON, XML, and tagged-binary readers and writers. JSON is declaration-driven and accepts reordered, missing, and unknown properties for forward-compatible interchange. The read side reports malformed input through fail; the write side serializes values according to their reflected fields and serialization attributes.

TagBin stores one readable document schema in the root header and one readable key for every reflected field. Declare Core.Serialization.Schema on persisted root types and keep that value stable across type or module renames. Declare Core.Serialization.Key before renaming a persisted field; the source identifier can then change while its single wire identity remains unchanged. Concrete structs stored through an interface always need a Core.Serialization.TypeKey, because their source type name is never used as a fallback identity.

#[Serialization.Schema("example.settings")] struct Settings { #[Serialization.Key("theme")] selectedTheme: String }

Keys are canonical rather than aliases: a field or struct type accepts one identity, and stored documents should be rewritten deliberately when that identity changes.

Treat external input as untrusted. Keep parsing errors at the boundary, add the filename or protocol context there, and only pass validated values into the rest of the program.

Time and concurrency

Core.Time.Duration represents an interval expressed in seconds. Core.Time.Timestamp represents a wall-clock instant as ticks, while Core.Time.DateTime exposes its calendar components. Use Core.Time.Stopwatch for elapsed-time measurement and Core.Time.FrameTiming for frame loops.

Concurrency is split into layers, and the shared worker pool is not one of Core's: tasks and parallel loops belong to the runtime.

NeedAPI
Independent work on the shared poolparallel for, Swag.Task, Swag.TaskGroup
A dedicated operating-system threadCore.Threading.Thread
Mutual exclusion, events, and read/write lockingCore.Sync
Lock-free counters and valuesCore.Atomic

Prefer a runtime task for independent CPU work: one process has one worker budget, whichever module submits to it. Use a dedicated thread for a long-lived blocking activity or a subsystem that requires thread affinity. Keep critical sections small and never retain a pointer into a container while another thread may resize that container.

Time values have different clocks and purposes. Wall-clock dates can change when the system clock is adjusted; elapsed-time measurements should use the monotonic timer exposed by the timing APIs.

Mathematics, reflection, and diagnostics

Core.Math contains scalar functions, vectors, matrices, rectangles, transforms, curves, and geometric algorithms. Floating-point comparisons and normalization helpers make their tolerance explicit; choose the tolerance that matches the scale of the data rather than relying on exact equality.

Core.Reflection inspects Swag type information, attributes, fields, enum cases, and arrays at runtime. Reflection values describe compiled program metadata. Do not mutate application storage through reflected pointers unless the API explicitly exposes a writable value.

For program output and diagnostics:

PurposeAPI
Terminal input and outputCore.Console
Programmer assertionsSwag.assert
Debugger interactionCore.Debugger
Process, arguments, and environmentCore.Env
Hardware informationCore.Hardware
Standard system errorsCore.Errors

Assertions protect programmer invariants; they are not a substitute for handling invalid files, user input, or operating-system failures. Public operations that can encounter those conditions report them through fail.

Use Swag.assert(condition, message) without a Core import. The message is optional. Swag.SafetyWhat.Assert controls assertion emission through BuildCfg.safetyGuards and Swag.Safety overrides: enabled in devmode and disabled in release by default. Disabled assertions evaluate none of their arguments, so keep required side effects outside them. Core.ASSERT is deprecated; query the local setting with #safety(Swag.SafetyWhat.Assert). The former Std.Core.Assert tag is replaced by the safety flag. #assert remains an unconditional compile-time check.

JSON and globalization

The reflection-driven JSON codec reads and writes ordinary Swag structs without a schema or annotations. Fields marked Core.Serialization.NoSerialize stay out of the document. The reader accepts properties in any order, retains initialized values for missing properties, and ignores properties the current declaration does not know, which lets configuration files evolve.

using Core struct Settings { title: String retries: u32 = 3 } let source: String = #raw """{"futureOption":true,"title":"Workbench"}""" var decoder: Serialization.Decoder'Serialization.Read.Json let settings = try decoder.readAll'Settings(source.toSlice())! defer Memory.delete(settings) var encoder: Serialization.Encoder'Serialization.Write.Json encoder.serializer.options.saveBlanks = true var output: ConcatBuffer try encoder.writeAll(&output, settings[])

Malformed UTF-8, invalid escapes and numbers, duplicate properties, trailing commas, excessive nesting, and data after the root value fail with a Core.Errors.SyntaxError. The decoder owns the returned struct; release it with Core.Memory.delete. Because JSON has no representation for NaN or infinity, the writer emits null for non-finite floating-point values.

Culture-aware presentation

Core.Globalization.CultureInfo groups number, currency, date/time, collation, plural, and case rules for one BCP 47 locale name. Pass a culture explicitly through application code when output must be deterministic. Core.Globalization.currentCulture remains available for process-wide defaults used by the existing numeric conversion routines.

using Core let culture = Globalization.CultureInfo.fromName("fr-FR") let amount = culture.currencyFormat.format(12345.5, culture.numberFormat) let when = culture.dateTimeFormat.formatDateTime(Time.DateTime{2026, 8, 13, 18, 30}) let form = culture.cardinalPlural(2)

The built-in profiles cover common conventions for English, French, German, Hindi, Turkish, Russian, Arabic, Japanese, Swedish, Polish, and Czech. Unknown locale names use invariant English display data and general plural rules; applications that need exhaustive CLDR tailoring can keep that policy above this compact core layer.

Simd.clmulHighLow

Multiplies the high lane of x by the low lane of y without carries, into a full 128-bit product.

Simd.clmulLowHigh

Multiplies the low lane of x by the high lane of y without carries, into a full 128-bit product.

Simd.clmulLowLow

Multiplies the low lanes of x and y without carries, into a full 128-bit product.

Simd.countTrue

Counts the mask lanes that are all-ones.

Simd.deinterleaveEven

Collects the even lanes of x then those of y, undoing one interleave.

Simd.deinterleaveOdd

Collects the odd lanes of x then those of y.

Simd.gather

Reads four signed 32-bit values through four unsigned indices.

Simd.interleaveHigh

Alternates lanes from the high halves of two vectors.

Simd.interleaveLow

Alternates lanes from the low halves of two vectors.

Simd.load

Reads one vector from memory; the pointer needs no particular alignment.

Simd.maximum

Returns the largest lane, with the NaN behavior of Core.Math.Simd.minimum.

Simd.minimum

Returns the smallest lane.

Simd.mulAddPairs

Multiplies 16-bit lanes pairwise and adds each pair of adjacent products into a 32-bit lane.

Simd.mulHigh

Returns the high half of every lane product, the bits above the lane width that * drops.

Simd.mulWidenHigh

Returns the exact products of the high half of the lanes, in lanes twice as wide.

Simd.mulWidenLow

Returns the exact products of the low half of the lanes, in lanes twice as wide.

Simd.packSigned

Narrows two vectors into one with signed saturation.

Simd.packUnsigned

Narrows two vectors into one with unsigned saturation.

Simd.permute

Permutes lanes: result lane i takes the lane its pattern lane names.

Simd.permute2

Permutes lanes out of two vectors: an index below the lane count reads x,

Simd.select

Blends two vectors through a mask: lanes of ifTrue where the mask lane is

Simd.shuffle

Permutes bytes through a dynamic table.

Simd.splat

Fills every lane with one scalar.

Simd.store

Writes one vector to memory; the pointer needs no particular alignment.

Simd.storeLow4

Writes the low four bytes of a byte vector to memory, as one 32-bit move.

Simd.storeLow8

Writes the low eight bytes of a byte vector to memory, as one 64-bit move.

Simd.subSaturating

Subtracts per lane with saturation: results clamp to the lane range instead of wrapping.

Simd.sum

Adds every lane into one scalar, with wrapping arithmetic for integers.

Simd.sumAbsoluteDifferences

Sums the absolute differences of all sixteen bytes.

Simd.sumWide

Sums every lane into a wider accumulator, which no lane width can overflow.

Simd.transpose4x4

Transposes four rows of four 32-bit lanes in place, through the interleave

Simd.transpose8x8

Transposes eight rows of eight 16-bit lanes in place, through three

Simd.truncateToS32

Converts float lanes to signed 32-bit integers by truncating toward zero.

Simd.widenHigh

Extends the high half of the lanes to double width, zero-extended for unsigned

Simd.widenLow

Extends the low half of the lanes to double width, zero-extended for unsigned

struct Core.Array #src

A growable, contiguous array of elements of type T.

The array owns its elements and its buffer, which grows as elements are added and is released when the array is dropped. Growth can move the elements and invalidates every pointer and slice borrowed from the array.

An array is a header over a memory block, and that header is part of its contract: the serializers, the reflection helpers and the formatters build one over storage they already own. Writing count is also how a caller truncates without dropping the elements, which clear and resize deliberately do not do. So these fields stay writable, unlike the state of a type that maintains an invariant across its fields.

struct Core.ByteSink #src

Writes the bytes of a stream to a file or to memory, through one cursor and one window.

An encoder receives one of these and appends to it piece by piece. A file sink holds one small write window and never accumulates the stream, so writing a long one costs the memory of one piece rather than the memory of the result; a piece larger than the window goes straight to the file.

A memory sink borrows its destination buffer: keep it valid and write to it only through the sink until closing it. It holds the whole stream, which only a bounded result should ask for.

struct Core.ByteSource #src

Reads the bytes of a stream held in a file or in memory, through one cursor and one window.

A decoder receives one of these and never learns which backing it has: the same reads, seeks, and peeks work on both. A file source keeps one read window alive and nothing else, so decoding costs the same memory whether the file holds ten frames or ten hours of them, and a read larger than the window goes straight to its destination rather than through it.

A memory source borrows its bytes: they must stay valid and unchanged until the source is closed. Core.ByteStream is the cursor for bytes that are already in memory; this is what a codec reads a file of any size through.

A read that runs past the end of the stream fails with Core.Errors.InvalidFormatError, because a decoder computing such an offset is reading a truncated stream.

Unlike Core.Guid128, a random Guid64 cannot provide UUID-level collision resistance. Use it for local object identities and temporary names, not as a security token or a globally coordinated database key.

struct Core.HashSet #src

An open-addressing hash set of unique keys.

Lookups, insertions, and removals take expected constant time. The set grows by rehashing, which moves every key and invalidates every entry pointer borrowed from it.

Fields

NameTypeDescription

The total number of slots in the hash table.

The number of valid elements currently in the set.

Methods

NameDescription

Adds key unless it is already present, and returns its entry.

Drops every key and leaves the set empty, keeping its slots for reuse.

Returns whether the set contains key.

free

Drops every key, releases the slots, and leaves the set empty.

isEmpty

Returns whether the set contains no elements.

opCount

Returns the number of elements in the set.

opDrop

Drops every key and releases the slots.

opPostCopy

Gives a copied set its own slots holding copies of the keys.

opSet

Replaces the content with copies of the keys in slice, ignoring duplicates.

opVisit

Visits every key in storage-slot order, binding it to key.

remove

Removes key; does nothing when it is absent.

reserve

Grows the set to at least newCapacity slots, rehashing every key.

reversed

Returns an immutable zero-allocation view that scans occupied slots in reverse order.

Adds key when it is absent or removes it when present, and returns whether it is now present.

struct Core.String #src

struct Crypto.Poly1305 #src

Authenticates a message under a one-time key, following RFC 8439.

A Poly1305 key authenticates exactly one message. Reusing it across two messages lets an observer recover the key material and forge tags, which is why Core.Crypto.chacha20Poly1305Seal derives a fresh one from each nonce.

struct Directory.Watcher #src

Owns a cancellable stream of filesystem changes for one directory tree.

Core.Directory.Watcher.next has at most one outstanding host read. A timeout preserves that request, so the next call continues waiting without a notification gap. cancel may be called from another thread and permanently changes subsequent reads to Cancelled. close releases resources and must not race with next or another close.

struct Env.Process #src

Owns a started child process, its pipes, and everything captured from it.

Start one with Core.Env.startProcess and drive it, or use Core.Env.runProcess to start it and wait for it in one step. The value closes every handle it still owns when it leaves scope, so a process is never leaked by an early return.

Text captured from a redirected stream accumulates inside the value and outlives Core.Env.Process.close, which is what lets a run be inspected after the child is gone.

Attention

A pipe holds a bounded amount of data, so a child that writes more than that blocks until this side reads it. Every wait on this type drains the redirected streams while it waits, which is what keeps the pair from deadlocking; a caller that waits on the platform handle by other means loses that guarantee.

#[Swag.NoCopy] struct Process

struct Env.ProcessEnvironment #src

Holds the environment variables a child process is started with.

A Core.Env.StartInfo naming no environment lets the child inherit the one of the current process unchanged. Start from Core.Env.currentEnvironment to add or override a few variables, or from an empty value to give the child exactly what it lists and nothing else.

Names follow the rule of the platform: Windows compares them without regard to case and stores them folded, so setting path there replaces the Path the system reported instead of adding a second variable beside it. A platform that distinguishes the case keeps a name as given.

var environment = Env.currentEnvironment() environment.set("SWAG_PATH", "c:/swag/bin") var info = Env.StartInfo{fileName: "swc.exe", arguments: "test", environment: &environment} let process = try Env.runProcess(info)
struct ProcessEnvironment

Methods

NameDescription
clear

Removes every variable, leaving the environment empty.

Returns how many variables the environment holds.

remove

Removes name. Removing a name the environment does not hold does nothing.

Binds name to value, replacing any previous binding.

struct Env.ProcessResources #src

What a measured process and everything it started consumed.

Answered by Core.Env.Process.resources once the process was started with StartInfo.measureResources. The whole tree is accounted, not just the process that was named: a program that does its work in helpers it spawns would otherwise report almost nothing.

The peaks are the highest each figure ever reached, so they stay meaningful after the processes that produced them are gone. Times are totals across the tree.

struct Env.StartInfo #src

Describes the process to start and how it is connected to the current one.

Only fileName is required. The executable is looked up the way the system resolves a command line, so a bare name is searched in the current directory and along the executable search path; pass a full path to remove the ambiguity.

How the child writes standard output.

Directory the child starts in, or null to inherit the current one.

Field details

consoleWindow#

Whether a console child may be given a console of its own.

A console program started from another console program shares the one already there and opens nothing either way, so this decides only what happens when there is none to share: a windowed program starting a console one. The system then builds a console and the host process that draws it, which flashes a window and can cost several times what the child itself costs — a price worth paying for a child the caller wants a reader to watch, and pure waste for one whose streams are already redirected here.

struct File.TweakFile #src

Fills registered struct instances from a line-oriented tweak text.

A line /Name selects the folder whose struct is named Name, with or without its namespace. Every other line assigns one field, name value, where name reaches into a nested struct through . and value can be $other to copy another field of the same folder once the whole text is read. Empty lines and lines starting with # are ignored, and a # after a value starts a comment. Lines that precede any folder line fill the last registered folder.

The registered instances are borrowed and must outlive the parsing calls.

struct Math.Curve #src

A curve of arbitrarily many keys, evaluated as one ordinate for one abscissa.

A curve is authored inside the unit square, and Core.Math.Curve.evaluateNormalized answers in that space. startX, endX, startY and endY map that square onto whatever range a caller works in, so one authored shape drives seconds, pixels or degrees through Core.Math.Curve.evaluate without being re-authored.

Every key owns its two tangents and the interpolation of the segment leaving it, so one curve expresses a smooth ease, a stepped hold and a corner at once — any shape, broken or not. The type is a plain aggregate over a Core.Array: it copies, serializes and drops like any other value.

struct Curve

Fields

NameTypeDescription
endXf32

Abscissa mapped from normalized one; defaults to one.

endYf32

Ordinate mapped from normalized one; defaults to one.

keysCore.Array'(Core.Math.CurveKey)

Keys of the curve, kept sorted by ascending abscissa.

startXf32

User-space window the normalized unit square maps onto.

startYf32

Ordinate mapped from normalized zero; defaults to zero.

Field details

keys#

Keys of the curve, kept sorted by ascending abscissa.

Core.Math.Curve.addKey maintains that order. Editing a key in place is allowed, and is how a curve editor retimes one; call Core.Math.Curve.sortKeys afterwards when the edit moved a key past a neighbour.

startX#

User-space window the normalized unit square maps onto.

Core.Math.Curve.evaluate reads an abscissa between startX and endX and answers an ordinate between startY and endY. The defaults leave both axes normalized, and an end below its start mirrors that axis.

Constants

NameDescription
NeutralWeight

Handle length at which a Bezier segment draws exactly the Hermite segment of the same

Methods

NameDescription
addKey

Inserts key at its place in abscissa order and returns the index it landed on.

bezierBounds

Returns the axis-aligned bounding box of the cubic Bézier curve from start to end whose control points are ctrl0 and ctrl1.

clear

Removes every key, leaving the user-space window untouched.

Returns the classic curve named by preset, owned by the caller and free to edit.

createBezier

Returns the curve of the cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) form used by style sheets.

Returns the user-space ordinate at the user-space abscissa x.

Returns the point at the parameter t of the quadratic Bézier curve from start to end whose control point is ctrl.

Returns the ordinate at x in the authored unit square.

evaluatePolynomial

Returns the cubic polynomial p0 * t³ + p1 * t² + p2 * t + p3 evaluated at t, component by component.

Returns whether the curve holds no key at all.

Removes the key at index, keeping the remaining ones in order.

setRange

Maps the normalized unit square onto a user-space window.

setTangent

Gives the key at index one slope on both sides, making the curve smooth across it.

setTangents

Gives the key at index two different slopes, breaking the curve into a corner.

setWeights

Sets the Bézier handle lengths of the key at index, as fractions of their segment.

shared

Returns the process-wide instance of a classic curve, borrowed rather than owned.

smoothTangents

Recomputes every tangent from the neighbours of its key, leaving no corner behind.

sortKeys

Restores the abscissa order after keys were edited in place.
struct Math.CurveKey #src

One control point of a Core.Math.Curve.

A key carries an arriving and a leaving tangent. Giving them the same value makes the curve smooth across the key; giving them different values breaks it into a corner, which is how a bounce lands and rebounds. Both are slopes, in ordinate units per abscissa unit, so they keep their meaning when a neighbouring key moves.

struct CurveKey

Fields

NameTypeDescription
inTangentf32

Slope of the segment arriving at the key.

Interpolation of the segment leaving this key.

inWeightf32

Length of the arriving Bézier handle, as a fraction of the segment width.

outTangentf32

Slope of the segment leaving the key.

outWeightf32

Length of the leaving Bézier handle, as a fraction of the segment width.

xf32

Abscissa of the key, normally inside the unit interval.

yf32

Ordinate of the key, free to leave the unit interval.

struct Math.Rectangle #src

Stores an axis-aligned rectangle as its top-left corner and its size.

Y grows downward: y is the top edge and Core.Math.Rectangle.bottom is y + height. A rectangle is normalized when neither dimension is negative, which most operations assume; Core.Math.Rectangle.normalize restores it.

struct Math.Transform2 #src

Stores a 2D affine transform as a 3 by 2 matrix applied to row vectors.

A point (x, y) maps to (x m11 + y m21 + tx, x m12 + y m22 + ty): the first two rows rotate, scale, and skew, and the last row translates.

struct Parser.RegExp #src

A compiled regular expression.

A pattern is compiled once and then matched against as many subjects as needed. Compiling is the only step that can fail; every match operation answers rather than fails.

var expr = try Parser.RegExp.create(#raw "(\d+)-(\w+)") if expr.match("42-answer") { Swag.assert(expr.getCapture(1) == "42") Swag.assert(expr.getCapture(2) == "answer") }

A search takes time proportional to the length of the subject, whatever the pattern: the engines behind it explore every branch of the pattern at once rather than one after another, so no pattern and no subject can make one search cost exponentially more than another. The one exception is a backreference, which no automaton can decide: a pattern that uses one is searched by trying the branches in turn, with a bound on how far that goes.

Every operation reports what it found in the last subject it was given: Core.Parser.RegExp.getCapture and Core.Parser.RegExp.captures return slices of that subject, and they stay valid only as long as it does. A failed match clears them.

The supported syntax is:

.any scalar value, line feed included
* + ?zero or more, one or more, zero or one
{n} {n,} {n,m}exactly, at least, or between that many repetitions
*? +? ?? {n,m}?the same, preferring the shortest match
`a\b`either side
(...)capturing group
(?:...)group that does not capture
(?<name>...)capturing group with a name, also spelled (?'name'...) and (?P<name>...)
(?i) (?m) (?s)case-insensitive, multi-line, dot-matches-line-feed, for the rest of the group
(?i:...)the same, for one group only
[abc] [a-z]any of those scalar values
[^abc]any scalar value but those
[[:alpha:]]a POSIX class: alnum, alpha, ascii, blank, cntrl, digit, graph, lower, print, punct, space, upper, word, xdigit
\d \w \s \l \udigit, word, space, lower-case and upper-case classes; the upper-case spelling of each is its complement
\pL \p{Lu}a Unicode property: L, Ll, Lu, Lt, N, Nd, S, Sm, Z, White_Space; \P is its complement
^ $start and end of the subject, or of a line under (?m)
\A \zstart and end of the subject, whatever the flags
\b \Bat a word boundary, and anywhere but at one
\n \t \x41 \x{1F600}one scalar value by escape, by hexadecimal byte, or by hexadecimal code point
\1 to \9what that capture group matched
#[Swag.Opaque] struct RegExp

struct Read.Json #src

Reads declaration-driven JSON objects independently of property order.

Missing fields retain their initialized value and unknown properties are ignored. Duplicate properties, malformed numbers, trailing commas, and trailing root data fail. Strings support every JSON escape, including UTF-16 surrogate pairs in \uXXXX escapes.

struct Read.TagBin #src

Reads the TagBin binary format, which keys every field so a stream survives the evolution of its types.

A stream written by version V of a type reads into version V+1 after these changes:

  • A new field. It keeps its default value.
  • A removed field. The stored value is ignored.
  • Reordered fields, as long as their names and types are the same.
  • A renamed field that declares a stable Core.Serialization.Key.

These type changes are supported:

  • Conversion between integer, float, rune, and Boolean types.
  • A new underlying type for an enum.
  • A new size for a static array.
  • Conversion from a static array to a Core.Array, and back.
  • Conversion from a single value to a static array or a Core.Array, and back.
  • A renamed interface implementation that declares a stable Core.Serialization.TypeKey.
  • An existing complex type that becomes Core.Serialization.Final.

These attributes are supported:

  • Core.Serialization.Version: the struct version, exposed while reading through Core.Serialization.Read.TagBin.version.
  • Core.Serialization.Schema: identifies and validates a root document independently from its type name.
  • Core.Serialization.Key: gives one stable identity to a field.
  • Core.Serialization.TypeKey: gives one stable identity to a serialized struct type.
  • Core.Serialization.Final: loads and saves the struct without versioning, faster and smaller.

The persisted format is version 1. Earlier experimental layouts are not accepted.

struct Read.Xml #src

Reads XML whose element order matches the serialized Swag type.

Every struct field is an element named after the field, and the document root is one more element around them, whatever its name, after an optional <?xml ...?> declaration. A sequence holds native values separated by blanks. Unknown, missing, and reordered elements fail. The input slice is borrowed until decoding completes.

struct Resources.Bundle #src

Resolves a resource name through an ordered chain of providers.

A resource is a run of bytes addressed by a relative name such as theme/widgets.png. Names always use / as separator, whatever the platform. Disk folders are searched first, in registration order, so a folder dropped next to the executable overrides what a module embeds; embedded bytes come last, which guarantees that a registered name always resolves.

var bundle: Resources.Bundle bundle.addEmbedded("lang/fr/app.tweak", EmbeddedFrench) bundle.addFolder("datas") let bytes = try bundle.load("lang/fr/app.tweak")

struct Serialization.Encoder #src

Encodes reflected Swag values through a format backend such as Core.Serialization.Write.TagBin or Core.Serialization.Write.Json.

var buf: ConcatBuffer var encoder: Encoder'Write.TagBin try encoder.writeAll(&buf, myStruct) try File.writeAllBytes(file, buf)

Can be serialized:

  • All simple types: bool/u8/u16/u32/u64/s8/s16/s32/s64/rune/f32/f64
  • A type value typeinfo, which will be saved as a CRC.
  • An interface. TagBin stores the concrete struct's stable Core.Serialization.TypeKey and value.
  • A struct.
  • A Core.String.
  • A Core.Array of valid values.
  • A static array of valid values.
Note

Type string is not supported. Consider using Core.String instead.

A struct can implement Core.Serialization.ISerialize to drive its own serialization. Otherwise it is saved field by field.

struct Serialization.Plan #src

Precomputed serialization plan of one struct type.

A plan is built once per type and shared by every encoder and decoder afterwards. It carries the filtered field list (fields marked Core.Serialization.NoSerialize are absent), the struct version, and the properties that select the wire layout of the struct. The field list, in order, is also the wire shape of the struct: the TagBin format stores it once per stream and references it from every instance.

Serializes access to shared data between threads.

NameTypeDescription
v*void?

Native lock state, managed by the methods.

Releases the mutex held by the calling thread.
struct Sync.RWLock #src

Lets many threads read shared data at once while one thread at a time writes it.

The lock is not reentrant, in either mode. Core.Sync.scopedLock and Core.Sync.sharedLock pair each acquisition with its release.

Fields

NameTypeDescription
v*void?

Native lock state, managed by the methods.

Methods

NameDescription
lock

Acquires the lock exclusively, like Core.Sync.RWLock.lockExclusive.

lockExclusive

Acquires the lock exclusively, waiting until no other thread holds it.

lockShared

Acquires the lock for shared access, waiting while a writer holds it.

tryLockExclusive

Acquires the lock exclusively when it is free and returns whether it did, without waiting.

tryLockShared

Acquires the lock for shared access when no writer holds it and returns whether it did, without waiting.

unlock

Releases an exclusive hold, like Core.Sync.RWLock.unlockExclusive.

unlockExclusive

Releases the exclusive hold of the calling thread.

unlockShared

Releases a shared hold of the calling thread.

enum Math.CurveInterpolation #src

Selects how the segment leaving one key reaches the next one.

The mode belongs to the key the segment starts at, so a single curve can hold a stepped hold, a straight ramp and a smooth ease at once.

enum CurveInterpolation

Cases

NameDescription
Bezier

Cubic Bézier along the tangents, over the handle lengths the weights ask for.

Constant

Holds the ordinate of the starting key until the next key.

Hermite

Cubic leaving and entering along the tangents, with neutral handle lengths.

Linear

Straight line between the two keys; ignores both tangents.

Smooth

Smoothstep between the two keys; ignores both tangents.
enum Math.CurvePreset #src

Names one classic curve, the shape a caller asks for instead of authoring it.

The last five leave the unit interval on purpose: an anticipating or overshooting shape passes beyond its endpoints before settling on them.

enum CurvePreset

Cases

NameDescription
EaseIn

Accelerates from rest.

EaseInBack

Draws back below zero, then accelerates.

EaseInOut

Accelerates, then decelerates symmetrically.

EaseInOutBack

Draws back, accelerates, overshoots, then settles.

EaseOut

Decelerates toward rest.

EaseOutBack

Overshoots one, then settles onto it.

EaseOutBounce

Lands on one and rebounds with decreasing height.

EaseOutElastic

Springs past one and oscillates onto it.

Linear

Keeps the ordinate proportional to the abscissa.

Methods

NameDescription
evaluate

Returns the ordinate of this classic shape at the abscissa x, which is clamped to the unit interval.

enum Text.Encoding #src

How the bytes of a text file spell their characters.

A reader meets these five families and nothing else in practice: UTF-8 everywhere, UTF-16 from Windows APIs and exports, UTF-32 from a few Unix pipelines, and one single-byte page for everything written before any of them. Windows1252 stands for that page: it is a superset of Latin-1 that differs only in 0x80-0x9F, where Latin-1 has unused controls and Windows put the quotation marks and dashes an actual document uses.

enum Encoding

Cases

NameDescription
Utf16Be

Two bytes per unit, most significant first.

Utf16Le

Two bytes per unit, least significant first, surrogate pairs above the BMP.

Utf32Be

Four bytes per character, most significant first.

Utf32Le

Four bytes per character, least significant first.

Utf8

Variable width, one to four bytes per character.

Windows1252

One byte per character, code page 1252.

enum Write.TagBinValueFlags #src

Additional signature for each value in an ad-hoc section, stored after its key and static type identity.

These numbers are the on-disk format, so both cases are pinned. Every element ever written carries bit 0, which is why Core.Serialization.Write.TagBinValueFlags.None is one rather than zero; renumbering them makes an existing stream decode its plain values as compressed ones.

#[Swag.EnumFlags] enum TagBinValueFlags: u8

Cases

NameDescription
Compressed

The value payload is deflate compressed.

None

No value option is enabled.

const ByteSink.WindowSize #src

Size of the write window of a file sink, in bytes.

Markers and headers are a few bytes each and would otherwise be one write call apiece; a piece of at least this size goes straight to the file instead.

const WindowSize = 64 * 1024'u64
const ByteSource.WindowSize #src

Size of the read window of a file source, in bytes.

It bounds the memory a source of any length uses, and it is the threshold from which a read goes straight to its destination instead of being copied twice.

const WindowSize = 64 * 1024'u64

func Array.storage #src

Returns the contiguous storage as a pointer the caller walks itself.

An empty array owns no block, and a caller asking an empty array for its storage is about to walk zero elements. The answer is then a dangling address, aligned for the element type and never read, rather than a null every caller would have to assert: walking is bounded by count, and a read through the dangling address faults exactly as loudly as a read through null. Ask isEmpty whether there is anything to walk, and toSlice when the walk should carry its own bounds.

The pointer is mutable whatever the receiver, exactly like reading the field was: a container that hands out its storage hands out the storage itself.

#[Inline] mtd const storage()->[*] T

func ByteSink.patch #src

Rewrites bytes this sink already accepted, at offset bytes from the start of its stream.

A container header carries totals a codec only learns once the last piece is written: a file size, a frame count, the size of the chunk holding the frames. Patching is how those fields are filled without holding the stream: the encoder writes a placeholder in the header, remembers where it went, and overwrites it here.

The patched range must lie entirely inside what the sink already wrote; a range reaching past the end fails rather than extending the stream. The write position is unchanged, so appending resumes exactly where it stopped.

func ByteSource.peek #src

Returns the bytes at the read position without consuming them.

The slice holds at least count bytes, and every further byte the source already holds after them: a memory source returns everything up to the end of the stream, a file source whatever its window covers. A scanner that walks frame headers therefore asks for the header it needs and reads ahead as far as the window goes at no cost. Fails when fewer than count bytes remain.

The slice borrows the source's own storage and stays valid until the next read, seek, skip, or peek on it. A file source grows its window to hold count bytes when they do not fit, so a caller bounds count to bound its memory.

func Crypto.argon2id #src

Derives a key from password and salt with Argon2id, RFC 9106, and fills destination with it.

Argon2id spends the first half of its first pass on data-independent addressing and everything after it on data-dependent addressing, which is what gives it both side-channel resistance and resistance to time-memory tradeoffs. It is the variant to choose unless an existing format demands another one.

salt holds at least 8 bytes and should hold 16. destination holds at least 4 bytes. parameters.memoryKib is at least eight times parameters.parallelism, and the derivation allocates that many kibibytes.

The same password, salt, parameters, and destination length always produce the same bytes, on every platform. Independent lanes share the runtime worker pool when their segments are large enough; the call joins them before returning or clearing memory.

var salt: [16] u8 try Crypto.randomBytes(salt) var key: [32] u8 try Crypto.argon2id("correct horse battery staple", salt, {memoryKib: 65536, iterations: 3, parallelism: 4}, key)
func argon2id(password, salt: const [..] u8, parameters: Argon2Parameters, destination: [..] u8) fail

Derives a key with Argon2id like the first overload, also binding secret and associatedData into it.

secret is the RFC 9106 key input: a value the verifier holds but the password database does not, at most 64 bytes. associatedData binds a context such as a user identifier. Both are optional, and both must be reproduced exactly to reproduce the tag.

func argon2id(password, salt, secret, associatedData: const [..] u8, parameters: Argon2Parameters, destination: [..] u8) fail
func Crypto.chacha20Block #src

Produces one IETF ChaCha20 key-stream block for counter.

Fails with Core.Errors.BadParameterError when key does not hold 32 bytes or nonce 12.

func chacha20Block(key: const [..] u8, counter: u32, nonce: const [..] u8)->[ChaCha20BlockSize] u8 fail
func Crypto.chacha20Poly1305Open #src

Verifies and decrypts ciphertext with ChaCha20-Poly1305, RFC 8439.

Returns whether the tag was valid. plaintext is only written when it was, so a caller never observes unauthenticated bytes. A false result means the key, the nonce, the associated data, the ciphertext, or the tag does not match what was sealed; it does not say which. A wrong tag size or a plaintext of another length than ciphertext also returns false. Fails with Core.Errors.BadParameterError when key does not hold 32 bytes or nonce 12.

func chacha20Poly1305Open(key, nonce, ciphertext, tag, associatedData: const [..] u8, plaintext: [..] u8)->bool fail
func Crypto.chacha20Poly1305Seal #src

Encrypts and authenticates plaintext with ChaCha20-Poly1305, RFC 8439.

key holds 32 bytes, nonce 12, tag 16, and ciphertext exactly as many bytes as plaintext. associatedData is authenticated but not encrypted; pass an empty slice when there is none. ciphertext and plaintext can be the same slice; any other overlap is not supported.

A nonce must never repeat under one key. Repeating it reveals the relationship between the two plaintexts and lets an observer forge tags for that key.

This is a single pass over the data in each direction, unlike encrypting and then authenticating with separate primitives. Fails with Core.Errors.BadParameterError when a buffer has the wrong size.

var nonce: [Crypto.ChaCha20Poly1305NonceSize] u8 try Crypto.randomBytes(nonce) var ciphertext: [5] u8 var tag: Crypto.Poly1305Tag try Crypto.chacha20Poly1305Seal(key, nonce, "hello", "", ciphertext, tag)
func chacha20Poly1305Seal(key, nonce, plaintext, associatedData: const [..] u8, ciphertext: [..] u8, tag: [..] u8) fail
func Crypto.chacha20Xor #src

XORs source with the IETF ChaCha20 key stream into destination.

The first block uses the key-stream counter initialCounter. Source and destination can be the same slice; other overlapping ranges are not supported. Large inputs share the runtime worker pool, and all output is complete before the call returns.

Fails with Core.Errors.BadParameterError when key does not hold 32 bytes, nonce 12, or destination as many bytes as source, and with Core.Errors.OverflowError when the input needs more blocks than the counter range starting at initialCounter provides.

func chacha20Xor(key, nonce, source: const [..] u8, destination: [..] u8, initialCounter = 0'u32) fail

func Crypto.pbkdf2HmacSha256 #src

Inserts key at its place in abscissa order and returns the index it landed on.

A key sharing the abscissa of an existing one is inserted after it. That is how a vertical jump is authored: the segment between the two is empty, so the later key takes over from that abscissa on.

The box is tight: it holds the extremes the curve actually reaches, not the control point.

func Curve.createBezier #src

Returns the curve of the cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) form used by style sheets.

The two handles are given as positions in the unit square, the way the CSS function spells them. Both abscissas are clamped to that interval, because a handle leaving it makes the curve stop being a function of its abscissa; the ordinates are free, which is what lets the form overshoot.

func createBezier(x1, y1, x2, y2: f32)->Curve
func Curve.evaluate #src

Returns the user-space ordinate at the user-space abscissa x.

This is Core.Math.Curve.evaluateNormalized read through the window Core.Math.Curve.setRange installed. A window with no width answers the first key, because every abscissa then names the same normalized position.

mtd const evaluate(x: f32)->f32
func Curve.evaluateBezier #src

Returns the point at the parameter t of the quadratic Bézier curve from start to end whose control point is ctrl.

The point is (1 - t)² * start + 2t(1 - t) * ctrl + t² * end. t runs from 0 at start to 1 at end and is not clamped.

func evaluateBezier(start, end, ctrl: Vector2, t: f32)->Vector2

Returns the point at the parameter t of the cubic Bézier curve from start to end whose control points are ctrl1 and ctrl2.

The point is (1 - t)³ * start + 3t(1 - t)² * ctrl1 + 3t²(1 - t) * ctrl2 + t³ * end. t runs from 0 at start to 1 at end and is not clamped.

func evaluateBezier(start, end, ctrl1, ctrl2: Vector2, t: f32)->Vector2
func Curve.evaluateNormalized #src

Returns the ordinate at x in the authored unit square.

An abscissa outside the keys is clamped onto the nearest one, so a curve never extrapolates a shape it was not given. A curve with no key answers zero.

mtd const evaluateNormalized(x: f32)->f32

Offers appName in the shell's Open with list for extension, for the current user, and returns whether every registry write succeeded.

The registered command runs appPath with the opened file, and the default application of the extension is left alone; Core.Env.claimFileExtension takes the extension over instead. Refused under a sandbox, which reports it as not associated: claiming a file extension changes what the shell does on the whole machine.

#[Swag.Discardable] func associateFileExtension(extension, appName, appPath: string)->bool
func Env.claimFileExtension #src

Makes appPath the program the shell runs for extension, for the current user.

This is the strong form of Core.Env.associateFileExtension: that one offers the application in the Open with list and leaves the default alone, which is what an application wants for a format it merely reads. This one takes the extension over, so opening one of those files — from a double-click, from cmd, from anywhere the shell resolves a document — runs appPath. Reserve it for an extension the application defines.

progId is the class name the extension points at, conventionally Vendor.Kind. It is what distinguishes this claim from another program's, so keep it stable: registering the same progId again updates the claim instead of adding a second one. description is the file type as the shell shows it in a folder listing.

The command it registers passes the opened file and then everything else the caller typed, so an extension claimed this way carries its own arguments.

Refused under a sandbox, which reports it as not claimed: this changes what the shell does on the whole machine.

#[Swag.Discardable] func claimFileExtension(extension, progId, description, appPath: string)->bool
func Env.corpusRoot #src

Returns the corpus root, or an empty string when the run was granted none.

func corpusRoot()->string
func Env.createWindow #src

Creates and owns a top-level application window.

The returned Core.Env.Window keeps its platform-specific state opaque and closes the window when it leaves scope. The logical options size is realized in the physical pixels of the monitor where the platform creates it.

func createWindow(options: WindowOptions)->Window fail
func Env.currentEnvironment #src

Returns the environment variables of the current process.

This is a snapshot: changing the returned value does not change the environment of the current process, only what a child started with it inherits.

func currentEnvironment()->ProcessEnvironment
func Env.deniedSystemMutations #src

Returns how many system mutations have been refused so far.

A smoke run reports this: an application that still reaches for the registry or the shell on startup is not yet isolated, even though nothing failed.

func deniedSystemMutations()->u64
func Env.enableDpiAwareness #src

Declares this process per-monitor DPI aware, so windows receive physical pixels.

Every window-creation path calls this before its first native window exists; an application only needs it directly when it creates native windows on its own. Once enabled, monitor and cursor coordinates are physical desktop pixels and the system no longer stretches window content on scaled displays. Repeated calls do nothing, and a failure (for example when the awareness was already set by other means) is ignored.

func enableDpiAwareness()
func Env.enterSandbox #src

Arms the sandbox at root, which becomes the answer to every special-directory query.

root is created when missing. Arming twice with the same root is accepted; changing an armed root is not, because code may already hold paths derived from the previous one.

func enterSandbox(root: string) fail
func Env.executablePath #src

Returns the executable path reported as command-line argument zero.

Returns an empty string when the runtime did not provide any arguments.

func executablePath()->string
func Env.exit #src

Exits the current process, reporting exitCode to whoever waits on it.

The code is signed like everywhere else exit codes travel — Core.Env.Process.waitForExit, Core.Env.Process.exitCode, Core.Env.Process.kill — and is reinterpreted at the system boundary.

func exit(exitCode: s32)

Returns the current logical-to-physical desktop scale factor.

Returns snapshots of all active display monitors, ordered from left to right.

func getMonitors()->Array'Monitor
func Env.getSpecialDirectory #src

Returns the normalized path of a well-known system directory.

Under a sandbox this answers inside it, so an application reaches its own scratch copy of the documents or application-data folder without knowing anything about the isolation.

Returns an empty string when the directory cannot be resolved.

func getSpecialDirectory(what: SpecialDirectory)->String
func Env.getSystemMetric #src

Returns one virtual-desktop metric in physical pixels.

func Env.grantCorpus #src

Grants root as the corpus: the one directory outside the sandbox a run may still write.

A test keeps its reference data next to its own source, so recording one — creating a snapshot that does not exist yet, or leaving the produced one beside the reference it diverged from — means writing into the sources under test. The sandbox refuses that, and it is right to: the escape belongs to whoever launched the run, not to the test asking for it. swc test grants the module or workspace it is testing, and nothing else; the machine stays out of reach.

root must already exist. Granting twice with the same root is accepted; changing a granted root is not, because code may already hold paths derived from the previous one.

func grantCorpus(root: string) fail

Reports whether the process is a smoke run: the real program, bounded by its launcher.

Opens path with its system-default application.

The request is handed to the Windows shell and returns before the application finishes. The result reports whether the shell accepted the request; it does not report what the application subsequently did with the file.

func Env.openFileWith #src

Asks the platform to let the user pick which application opens path.

The chooser is the shell's own, so it offers the same applications, the same default-handler checkbox and the same store lookup the file explorer offers. It runs in its own process: the call returns as soon as the request is handed over, long before the user has chosen anything, and reports only whether the chooser could be started.

func Env.quoteArgument #src

Returns value spelled so the system parses it back as exactly one argument.

A value holding a space, a tab or a quote is wrapped, and the backslashes in front of a wrapping quote are doubled, which is what the command-line grammar needs to give the child the string that was passed here. Use it for any argument that comes from a path or from input rather than from a literal; Core.Env.joinArguments does it for a whole list.

func quoteArgument(value: string)->String

Returns the normalized path of a well-known system directory on the machine itself, ignoring any sandbox.

Reserved for code that genuinely has to reach the real system, such as locating a system executable to launch. Anything that reads or writes an application's own data must go through Core.Env.getSpecialDirectory instead, so a test cannot touch the real thing.

Returns an empty string when the directory cannot be resolved.

func Env.runProcess #src

Starts a process, waits for it to exit, and returns it with everything it produced.

Standard output and standard error are captured, so the returned value answers Core.Env.Process.standardOutput and Core.Env.Process.standardError as well as Core.Env.Process.exitCode. Standard input is inherited.

let process = try Env.runProcess("swc.exe", "--help") if process.exitCode() != 0 do fail Errors.BadParameterError{"the compiler refused to answer"} Swag.print(process.standardOutput())
func runProcess(fileName: string, arguments: string? = null)->Process fail

err is the value a catch binds. The text is read from the Swag.BaseError a standard error embeds as its first field; an error type without one, or with an empty message, answers with its type name instead, so the result is always printable. A null error answers with an empty string.

func Event.init #src

Creates an unnamed event in this value, which must not own one yet.

func Event.initNamed #src

Creates or opens a named event shared by processes in the current login session.

The event must be invalid on entry. name is borrowed only during this call, is case-sensitive, and must be nonempty without zero bytes or backslashes. On Windows, the name is resolved in the local session namespace. An existing event retains its reset mode and signaled state; manual and initState apply only when it is created. The default is an initially unsignaled event that releases one waiter per signal. Failure leaves this value invalid. Each opener owns its handle until release or drop; releasing one handle does not invalidate another opener's event.

mtd initNamed(name: string, manual, initState = false) fail

Opens a read-only stream that releases the file between operations.

Each read, seek, or size query reopens the path with read, write, and delete sharing. The cursor survives between calls, but the file may be replaced, truncated, or removed; subsequent operations observe the current path and can fail. No native handle is retained while idle, so even an exclusive writer can save the source. This is not a consistent snapshot.

mtd read(buffer: *void?, length: u64)->u64 fail

func FileStream.readTextChunk #src

Reads the next bounded segment of text in encoding and returns it as UTF-8.

The stream position advances by the bytes consumed, which is what the caller counts in: a segment of UTF-16 returns roughly half as many UTF-8 bytes as it consumed, so the returned length is never an offset. maxBytes needs at least four bytes so every character can make progress. An empty result means end of file.

No character is ever split across two calls: a UTF-8 sequence, a surrogate pair, or a wide unit cut by maxBytes is left for the next one. A malformed sequence is decoded to the replacement character rather than reported, except under Core.Text.Encoding.Utf8 where Core.File.FileStream.readUtf8Chunk answers and keeps its stricter contract.

mtd readTextChunk(maxBytes: u64, encoding: Text.Encoding)->String fail
func FileStream.readUtf8Chunk #src

Reads the next bounded UTF-8 segment without splitting an encoded rune.

The stream position advances by the returned byte count. maxBytes needs at least four bytes, so every UTF-8 rune can make progress. A malformed sequence at the current position leaves that position unchanged and reports Core.Errors.InvalidFormatError. An empty result means end of file.

mtd readUtf8Chunk(maxBytes: u64)->String fail

Formats a byte count as a compact human-readable size, such as "312 B", "4.10 KB" or "13.4 MB".

Units are 1024-based with the conventional KB/MB/GB/TB labels. Scaled values keep three significant digits; exact byte counts below 1 KB are printed unscaled.

func byteSize(bytes: u64)->String

Raises a compiler error when fmt does not have exactly one placeholder per value.

Formatting completes before the destination changes, so fmt and values may borrow it. The destination keeps its allocator and contains a null-terminated string, including when empty.

func replaceString(dest: *String, fmt: string, values: ...)
func Format.toInterp #src

Appends exp to buf, with each {expr} or {expr:format} replaced by the value of expr.

This is a mixin: the interpolated expressions are caller-side names, so the generated code must resolve in the caller scope; the internal locals use "#uniq?".

#[Mixin] func toInterp(buf: *ConcatBuffer, exp: string)

Returns a new Core.String holding exp interpolated like the overload that appends to a Core.ConcatBuffer.

#[Mixin] func toInterp(exp: string)->String
func Format.toString #src

Returns a new Core.String holding fmt with each % placeholder replaced by the next value.

Each % stands for the next value of values, and %% writes a single %.

let x = Format.toString("my life is %", myLife)

% can be followed by a format option between {}.

let x = Format.toString("my life in hexadecimal is %{X}", myLife)

%{#n} targets the 0-based argument n instead of the next one, so a translated format string can reorder its arguments. An indexed placeholder does not advance the running argument position, and it can carry a format option after :.

let x = Format.toString("%{#1} before %{#0:X}", 255, "written")
  • See Core.StrConv.ConvertFormatInt.setFormat for the integer format options.
  • See Core.StrConv.ConvertFormatFloat.setFormat for the floating-point format options.
func toString(fmt: string, values: ...)->String

func Geometry.closestPointsBetweenSegments #src

Returns the closest pair of points between two segments and the distance separating them.

first lies on the segment from firstStart to firstEnd, and second on the segment from secondStart to secondEnd. A segment whose ends coincide is treated as a point. When several pairs are equally close, as with overlapping parallel segments, one of them is returned.

func closestPointsBetweenSegments(firstStart, firstEnd, secondStart, secondEnd: Math.Vector2)->{ first: Math.Vector2, second: Math.Vector2, distance: f32 }
func Geometry.distanceFromPointToLine #src

Returns the distance from point to the infinite line through lineStart and lineEnd.

When the two points coincide there is no line, and the distance to lineStart is returned.

func distanceFromPointToLine(point, lineStart, lineEnd: Vector2)->f32
func Geometry.distanceFromPointToSegment #src

Returns the shortest distance from point to the segment from segmentStart to segmentEnd.

A segment whose ends coincide is treated as the point segmentStart.

func distanceFromPointToSegment(point, segmentStart, segmentEnd: Vector2)->f32
func Geometry.ellipseContainsPoint #src

Returns whether point lies inside or on the axis-aligned ellipse centered at center with the radii radiusX and radiusY.

Both radii must be positive, which is asserted.

func ellipseContainsPoint(point, center: Vector2, radiusX, radiusY: f32)->bool
func Geometry.intersectLines #src

Returns the point where the infinite line through start0 and end0 crosses the one through start1 and end1.

intersects is false, and point is zero, when the lines are parallel or coincident. The test compares the cross product of the two direction vectors with epsilon, so it depends on their lengths as well as on the angle between them.

func intersectLines(start0, end0, start1, end1: Vector2, epsilon: f32 = ConstF32.Epsilon)->{ intersects: bool, point: Vector2 }
func Geometry.intersectSegments #src

Returns the point where the segment from start0 to end0 meets the segment from start1 to end1.

intersects reports whether the segments meet, and point is only meaningful when they do. epsilon is the tolerance of both the parallelism test and the segment ends, so segments that touch at an end intersect. Collinear segments that overlap report one end of their overlap, and a segment whose ends coincide is treated as a point.

func intersectSegments(start0, end0, start1, end1: Vector2, epsilon: f32 = ConstF32.Epsilon)->{ intersects: bool, point: Vector2 }
func Geometry.polygonContainsPoint #src

Returns whether point lies inside the polygon whose vertices are polygon, in order.

The last vertex connects back to the first, and a self-intersecting polygon follows the even-odd rule. A point exactly on an edge may land on either side, and an empty polygon contains nothing. This is the PNPoly algorithm by W. Randolph Franklin.

func polygonContainsPoint(polygon: Array'Math.Vector2, point: Math.Vector2)->bool
func Geometry.triangleContainsPoint #src

Returns whether point lies inside or on an edge of the triangle a, b, c.

The vertices may be given in either winding order: the point is inside when it lies on the same side of all three edges.

func triangleContainsPoint(point, a, b, c: Vector2)->bool

func Hash.hash32 #src

Returns a 32-bit hash of value.

A string hashes its bytes with Core.Hash.hashBytes32. A struct that implements Core.Hash.IHash32 or Core.Hash.IHash64 supplies its own hash; another struct hashes its bytes, skipping the dynamic identity slots it contains. Integers use a multiplicative hash, and other values hash their bits.

#[ConstExpr, Safety(.All, false)] func(T) hash32(value: T)->u32
func Hash.hash64 #src

Returns a 64-bit hash of value.

A string hashes its bytes. A struct that implements Core.Hash.IHash64 or Core.Hash.IHash32 supplies its own hash; another struct hashes its bytes, skipping the dynamic identity slots it contains. Other values hash their bits.

#[ConstExpr, Safety(.All, false)] func(T) hash64(value: T)->u64
func Hash.hashBytes32 #src

Returns a 32-bit hash of the bytes in buffer.

Tuned for the short keys a hash table actually stores. Core.Hash.Crc32 walks a lookup table one byte at a time below its 64 byte unrolled block, which dominates the cost of a table probe; this reads the buffer in 8 byte chunks, overlaps the tail instead of stepping through it, and never reads outside the range.

#[ConstExpr, Safety(.All, false)] func hashBytes32(buffer: const [..] u8?)->u32
func Hash.jenkins #src

Returns a well-distributed hash of the integer h.

The mix is cheap and spreads every input bit over the whole result, which suits hash-table keys that are already integers.

#[Safety(.All, false)] func jenkins(h: u64)->u64

Returns a well-distributed hash of the 32-bit integer h, using Robert Jenkins' mix.

#[Safety(.All, false)] func jenkins(h: u32)->u32
func Hash.murmur3 #src

Returns the MurmurHash3 finalizer mix of the integer h.

Every input bit affects every output bit, which suits hash-table keys that are already integers.

#[Safety(.All, false)] func murmur3(h: u32)->u32

Returns the MurmurHash3 64-bit finalizer mix of the integer h.

#[Safety(.All, false)] func murmur3(h: u64)->u64

Combines the hashes a and b into one hash.

Combines the 64-bit hashes a and b into one hash.

Returns a hash of the len bytes at key, seeded with seed.

The byte hash is MurmurHash64A, which reads the input in eight-byte blocks.

func Latin1.compare #src

Compares UTF-8 text in byte order, optionally ignoring ASCII and Latin-1 case pairs.

Returns -1, 0 or 1. Case-insensitive comparison folds A-Z and U+00C0-U+00DE except U+00D7 to their lowercase partners. Other encoded characters remain byte-exact; this performs neither full Unicode case folding nor Unicode normalization.

func compare(src, dst: const [..] u8, ignoreCase = false)->s32
func Latin1.compareNatural #src

Compares UTF-8 text naturally, returning -1, 0 or 1.

ASCII digit runs compare numerically and ASCII/Latin-1 whitespace is skipped. ignoreCase maps only ASCII and Latin-1 case pairs; other encoded characters remain byte-exact. No Unicode normalization is performed.

#[Swag.Sanity(Swag.SafetyWhat.All, false)] func compareNatural(src, dst: const [..] u8, ignoreCase = false)->s32

Maps exactly length bytes beginning at offset.

The range must fit in the file size sampled by this call. Empty regions are supported and own no native view. A non-empty region owns its view and a duplicate file handle, so it can be closed or flushed after this Core.File.MappedFile is closed.

func MappedFile.open #src

Opens an existing file for memory mapping.

ReadWrite enforces the process write sandbox. CopyOnWrite opens the underlying file for reading because private page changes never reach it.

func open(name: string, access = MapAccess.Read)->MappedFile fail
func MappedFile.openSnapshot #src

Copies a file to temporary storage and opens that copy for read-only mapping.

The copy uses a bounded buffer and releases the source before returning. Later writes, truncation, deletion, or replacement of the source do not affect the mapped bytes. The source must remain unchanged during the copy. Temporary storage is reclaimed after this value and its last region close. The returned name remains the original source path. maxBytes limits the copy to a prefix; zero creates an empty snapshot.

func openSnapshot(name: string, maxBytes = Swag.U64.Max)->MappedFile fail

Flushes shared writable pages and the duplicated file handle.

The operation does nothing for read-only and copy-on-write regions. A successful flush of a ReadWrite region makes both the mapped pages and file buffers durable according to the host filesystem's guarantees.

func MappedRegion.releasePages #src

Drops the pages holding bytes from the working set of the process.

A walk over a large mapped file touches every page it reads, and each page stays charged to the process until the system trims it: an index scan of a film reads gigabytes and looks, to a task manager, as if the program had allocated them. Releasing the pages a walk is done with keeps the memory the process reports at the size of what it still uses.

Nothing is lost. A released page comes back on its next access, from the file cache while the system still holds it, so this is a memory-accounting hint: it is safe on any readable range, mapped or not, does nothing for an empty one, and never fails. The pages are the whole ones containing bytes; a range that shares a page with data still in use keeps that page resident only until its next access.

func releasePages(bytes: const [..] u8)
